implementation_notes: TypeScript adds nothing to the JavaScript prefetch story (no CPU prefetch; the levers are typed arrays for locality and fetch priority / preload / Worker for overlap) - but the types make the network hints explicit and typed, and the type system documents that there is no CPU-level prefetch available. In a Node.js service, the analogous prefetch is warming a connection pool or a cache entry ahead of a request, which is a real latency win and is best expressed as an explicit typed function (prefetchUser(id): Promise<void>) rather than a hint. For CPU memory, a Float64Array over a number[] is the typed-array locality win. As everywhere in JavaScript, the dominant latency is network and main-thread jank, so the prefetch that pays is usually the network one or moving work off the main thread to a Worker.
idiom_name: no CPU prefetch; typed arrays for locality, fetch priority / preload for network, and explicit typed warm functions for connection/cache
pitfalls: No CPU prefetch exists in TypeScript; a number[] may be boxed - a Float64Array is the contiguous equivalent.
fetch priority is a Chromium-only hint, ignored elsewhere and not a guarantee of ordering.
prefetch / preload resource hints waste bandwidth if the resource is not actually used next.
A manual prefetch that is not awaited (fire-and-forget) can be cancelled by the runtime or race with the real request - make it an explicit typed warm you await or deliberately ignore.
